title: The fearless Formless
hook: Nanak says the Formless alone is fearless; all else is dust by comparison (Asa di Var, ang 464)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhau: wind, rivers, sun and kings, all moving in awe. And one alone without fear. Today we stand with that one line.

If you've been on this path since the first year, you know the word. It sits in the Mool Mantar, the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after the Creator and before without hate: nirbhau. Without fear. Yesterday's salok ended on it, after a whole universe of trembling: only the Formless is without fear. Today's salok, the next one in the var, starts there and refuses to move on quickly. Nanak, it says, the Formless is fearless. Then it looks at everything else people admire.
screen: `NIRBHAU, FROM THE MOOL MANTAR.` → `A UNIVERSE OF TREMBLING.` → `ONLY ONE WITHOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Two words carry this salok on ang 464. Nirbhau: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe we met yesterday. And nirankar: nir again, without, and akar, form or shape. The Formless. Together they answer a very human question: is there anything that isn't afraid? Everything else, yesterday's salok said, lives in awe. And anything with a form can break; it can be lost. The salok goes on to list what people admire and tell stories about, and sets each beside the Formless. So many celebrated figures are like dust. So many tales are told and retold, so many learned arguments made. People dance and sing for a crowd. Others wear earrings and necklaces worth a fortune, and the bodies that wear them, the salok says plainly, turn to ash. Then a turn worth noticing. Real wisdom isn't found through talk. Speaking of the One is as hard as iron. It comes by grace; cleverness and display only wear a person out. Here's why it matters. So much fear attaches to forms: a body getting sick, a job disappearing, a reputation cracking, a person leaving. The salok doesn't call those fears silly. Forms really do pass. What it offers is a place to stand. If only the Formless is fearless, then the way through fear, in Sikh teaching, isn't to become hard and fearless yourself. It's to stay close to the One who is. Some Sikh teachers put it in a short phrase: the one who fears the One fears nothing else.
screen: `NIR-BHAU: WITHOUT FEAR.` · `NIR-AKAR: WITHOUT FORM.` · `EVERY FORM CAN BREAK.` · `WISDOM COMES BY GRACE, NOT TALK.` · then, large: `ONLY THE FORMLESS IS FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Let one real fear come to mind, not the biggest, and notice the form it clings to: your health, your money, a person. Set it beside the whole sky, the wind and rivers moving in their order, and watch it take its true size; you don't have to make it disappear. If you pray, say nirbhau, nirankar, quietly.
Nirbhau, without fear: nir, without, and bhau, the fear and awe met yesterday, the word the Mool Mantar gives right after without hate.
Your line: only he is fearless. Forms pass; the Formless doesn't. Five hundred forty-four days now.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet the word nirbhau every day in the Mool Mantar, and hear this salok on the fearless Formless when Asa di Var is sung at dawn.

original.note: Gurmukhi: without fear, without form; nir- means without in both words.

what a scholar hears: nirbhau echoes the Mool Mantar; nir- plus akar gives nirankar, and the salok sets admired forms, jewels and learned talk against it.

chat.says: If only God is fearless, how am I supposed to deal with fear?
options: The salok's way isn't to grow hard yourself; it's to stay close to the fearless One.
The salok says fear means weak faith, so a real Sikh simply stops feeling it.
The salok says fear is silly, since jobs, health and people never really pass.
chat.meaning: Forms really do pass, the salok says. The way through fear is to stay close to the One who is fearless.

Mool Mantar.meaning: the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (Nanak nirbhau nirankar), Ang 464–465

notes: The salok names Ram and Kanh (Krishna) among those who are 'dust' beside the Formless. This script deliberately says only 'so many celebrated figures' so as not to set the salok against Hindu devotion; Keeper to confirm the approach.

Paraphrased content of the salok (tales told, learned arguments, people dancing and singing, jewels worth lakhs, bodies turning to ash, wisdom not found by talk, 'kathna karrha saar', grace): confirm order and ang (464–465).
The saying 'the one who fears the One fears nothing else' is offered as a common Sikh phrase, not a quotation; confirm or rephrase.
Gurmukhi spelling ਨਿਰੰਕਾਰੁ with aunkar as in the text; confirm.

Fresh review: 'a hundred times' and 'most of our fears' cut; the teach no longer puts 'everything with a form lives with fear' in Guru Nanak's mouth (the salok does not say it); the closing saying is now attributed to some Sikh teachers, not 'Sikhs often'.
